summary: A guide to enjoying summer produce, beginning with a six-step plan for growing a backyard fruit and vegetable garden and moving on to ways of eating and preserving the harvest. It covers tomatoes, berries, sweet corn, salads, canning and freezing, grilling, herbs and edible flowers, refreshing drinks, and involving kids in gardening. Advice is attributed to a range of gardeners, dietitians, and chefs.
one_line: A guide to growing a backyard summer garden and cooking, preserving, and enjoying the produce, with expert tips throughout.
key_facts: Garden expert Julia Matthews of the Greenthumb Gardening Society said, "There is something incredibly satisfying about plucking a sun-warmed tomato straight from the vine and enjoying it on the spot."
Vegetables such as bell peppers and zucchinis need at least 6-8 hours of direct sunlight daily.
Soil scientist Dr. Aaron Lee said on September 15 that "Healthy soil is the bedrock of a productive garden," and recommends a mix of nutrient-rich compost and potting soil.
Local farmer Emily Nguyen said on September 22 that planting basil near tomatoes enhances flavor and repels flies and mosquitoes; marigold plantings can also deter pests.
Tomato expert and author Tom Cartwright advised on September 29 that tomatoes are ready when they are a deep, even red and slightly soft to the touch.
Dietitian Laura Peterson notes that berries are packed with antioxidants and suggests infused water combinations like strawberry-basil or cucumber-mint.
Registered nutritionist Alexis Taylor suggests building salads on greens like arugula or spinach, adding chopped veggies, and a sweet fruit such as orange segments or mango.
A classic vinaigrette can be made with olive oil, vinegar, mustard, and a touch of honey.
Canning workshop leader Michael Johnston explained on September 10 that canning tomatoes, peaches, or berries lets you enjoy summer flavor in winter.
Freezing is an alternative to canning, and blanching vegetables before freezing helps preserve texture and color.
Dietitian Rachel Kim suggested on September 8 skewering bell pepper, onion, and zucchini and grilling over a medium flame to caramelize their natural sugars.
Farm-to-table chef Kelly Davidson recommends growing basil, mint, or cilantro, and edible flowers like nasturtiums or violets, which can thrive on windowsills or balcony planters.
Samantha Lee, a mother of three, said on September 18 that kids are more likely to try new foods when they've had a hand in growing them.
A cold brew tea can be made by steeping black or green tea with fresh fruit slices and herbs in the refrigerator overnight.
